title: That time when South Park introduced a new legal strategy
excerpt: The Chewbacca defense, a fictional courtroom strategy, and the real case behind the satire.
author: Shari Explains
coverAlt: Original cover artwork for That time when South Park introduced a new legal strategy
body:
## Background

“Chef Aid” is the fourteenth episode of the show’s second season. It aired on October 7, 1998, and follows a character named Chef who goes to court after a record company sues him for harassment. In this episode, the company hires famous lawyer Johnnie Cochran to represent them. Cochran uses the “Chewbacca defense,” which leads to Chef losing the case. Johnnie Cochran is a real-life attorney who is best known for representing O.J. Simpson when he was on trial for murder. The Chewbacca Defense is a parody of Cochran’s famous closing statement, “If the glove doesn’t fit, you must acquit!” which led to Simpson’s acquittal.

## Examples in the courtroom: O.J. Simpson murder trial

Cochran’s famous closing statement “If the glove doesn’t fit, you must acquit!” is the precursor for the Chewbacca defense. Simpson’s gloves were seen as key pieces of evidence for the prosecution as there were traces of both the 2 victims and Simpson’s blood.

## Examples in the courtroom: Tax fraud case in Jacksonville FL

In 2020, business owner Paul Berkins Moise was indicted by the IRS on tax fraud charges. In 2022, his case was brought to trial in which the defense argued that the revised calculations of Moise’s income and expenses should be deemed inadmissible, as the prosecution’s initial calculations were “so bad” they had to revise them. The prosecution argued that the initial calculations had nothing to do with the fact that Moise was on trial for tax fraud and claimed that the defense’s argument was an example of the Chewbacca defense. Moise was found guilty of his charges and tried to appeal his sentence, claiming prosecution misconduct. His appeal was denied.

## How to recognize red herrings

The Chewbacca defense is an example of a red-herring logical fallacy. This fallacy distracts from the main argument by introducing irrelevant information. Here are some tips to recognize a red herring!

1. Appeals to emotion rather than stating facts to back up their arguments

2. Distraction and confusion are used to divert attention and confuse jurors - the Chewbacca defense exploits cognitive bias, as when people are presented with confusing information, they are more likely to make choices that lead to the easiest outcome.

Example: Imagine you are on trial for theft. In closing statements, your defense attorney starts bringing up algebra and how the shop owner you (allegedly) stole from failed his 9th-grade algebra class. This would be seen as an example of the Chewbacca defense as your attorney brought up information that is irrelevant to the case.

## Criticisms

1. Not a legitimate legal strategy: Many lawyers have argued that the Chewbacca defense is not an actual legal strategy as it lacks a solid legal argument and focuses on confusing jurors rather than disproving evidence.

2. Seen as a weak legal technique

3. Unethical: The Chewbacca defense relies on the manipulation of the jury rather than legal reasoning

4. High risk: If the jury recognizes that the attorney is using the Chewbacca defense, their credibility in the trial can be damaged.

## From Shonda Mosby, practicing attorney

“When the defense lawyer does decide to put on a defense (call witnesses) they can put on "any defense" that is legally permissible, meaning they can present any argument or evidence that could potentially create reasonable doubt about their client's guilt, even if they believe their client is guilty, as long as it adheres to ethical standards and does not involve knowingly presenting false information to the court. So the idea of the Chewbacca defense (which is a fictional defense created for the television show South Park) really is a play on the extreme to which some (not most) lawyers will go to create reasonable doubt. However, even if a criminal defense lawyer attempts to present a so-called red-hearing fallacy, which is "a logical error that occurs when someone introduces an irrelevant topic to divert attention from the main issue," most judges will not allow them to do so because any evidence must be relevant. For instance, the scene in South Park involves the defense lawyer making the argument that "if Chewbacca living on Endor does not make sense—and if even mentioning Chewbacca in the case does not make sense—then the jury must acquit." This fictional example is an extreme version which would cause opposing counsel to object and the judge to most likely sustain the objection and strike the comment.

However, there are other ways that an attorney can deflect from the main issue of the case - whether their client did it - by pointing to the racism of the cops, talking about the bad behavior of the victim, or any issue that does not directly go to guilt. One of the main purposes of cross-examination- bias- can be considered a distraction because just because a witness is biased does not mean they are lying. One of the most obvious and everyday examples where this type of distraction is visible is in political commentary. When one side is faced with something critical to their point of view, they deflect to another problem. Last night, I was watching the news, and an AI video was shown that Trump posted of a luxury resort on the land that is now war-torn Gaza. The commentator asked a Trump ally if he agreed that the video was insensitive and disturbing because it ignores the people currently living there in the devastation. Rather than address the question, the person said it was disturbing when Hamas attacked innocent people. Both can be true, but the answer does not address the question. That is the basic premise of a "red herring fallacy.”

—Shonda Mosby, practicing attorney
